notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Luke 20:1–24. I couldn't find everything you asked for. I didn't find any Catholic or Orthodox reading of this passage (my searches turned up only general articles about the *Catena Aurea*), no netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes, nothing from Pentecostal sites or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, and Wesley's notes on chapter 20 cut off before the page reached it. Those gaps are left out below.

---

**v. 1**
- **Timing.** The Pulpit Commentary places this in Passion Week, probably on the Tuesday. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Precept Austin adds that John MacArthur thinks it was Wednesday, because he dates Palm Sunday to the Monday. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- **"Proclaiming the gospel."** Ellicott says the Greek verb ("to evangelise") is typical of Luke. Mark and John never use it, while Luke uses it ten times in the Gospel and fifteen in Acts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- **"Came up to Him."** Ellicott says the verb suggests a sudden, possibly planned move. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Utley (bible.org) says the same verb can mean "to assault." He identifies the three groups as the Sanhedrin. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- Guzik says Jesus didn't seek these debates. He wanted to teach the people the good news, and the questioners came to Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Precept Austin notes that groups who usually didn't get along joined forces against a common enemy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik says the leaders wanted to know by what right Jesus had cleared the temple, especially since He had no formal rabbinic training. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary sees a trap. If Jesus openly claimed a divine commission, they expected to convict him out of his own mouth of blasphemy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Utley calls authority a central question every person must face: about God, about Scripture and about Jesus. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**vv. 3–4**
- Guzik says Jesus wasn't dodging the question. If John was from God, he was right to proclaim Jesus as Messiah, and then Jesus had all authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary makes the same point: John had introduced Jesus to the people, so accepting John meant accepting the One he pointed to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Utley notes that neither John nor Jesus was an official scribe, yet the people recognised God's power in both. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 5**
- Utley says self-interest, not truth, drove their discussion. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 6**
- **"Stone us."** Ellicott says this is Luke's more vivid version of "we fear the people" in the other Gospels. He points to the attempts to stone Jesus and the stoning of Stephen as signs the crowd might really do it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Utley says the Greek for "convinced" shows the people held a settled view that John was a prophet. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 7**
- Guzik: their answer shows they cared more about winning the argument than knowing the truth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Utley: they had an opinion but wouldn't risk saying it publicly. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 8**
- Guzik: Jesus cared for sincere seekers but not for cynical manipulators. If we want answers from Him, we must first deal honestly with what God has already shown us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/

**v. 9**
- **The vineyard.** Guzik says Isaiah 5 uses the vineyard as a picture of Israel, and the tenants stand for the religious leaders. Tenant farming was common, and archaeologists have found records of similar disputes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Utley says the parable could refer to the nation (Isaiah 5) or to its leaders (v. 19). He calls it the strongest rejection of first-century Judaism in the New Testament. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- **"For a long time."** Ellicott says only Luke includes this phrase. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Gill says Luke leaves out the hedge, winepress and tower, which stand for the blessings Israel enjoyed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-9.htm

**v. 10**
- Utley says the landowner normally received a share of the crop. The tenants' repeated violence is the shocking twist. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- The Pulpit Commentary says that after all His care for the vineyard, God looked for fruits of gratitude and fidelity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: only Luke stresses the repeated phrase "sent him away empty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm

**v. 12**
- **"Wounded."** Ellicott says this verb is found only in Luke and has a "half-surgical ring." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Utley says the English word "trauma" comes from it. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 13**
- **"Perhaps."** Ellicott says only Luke's account includes this note of doubt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the owner's question "What shall I do?" recalls Genesis 1:26, and that the verse shows the Gospel writers' high view of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Utley links "beloved son" to the Father's words at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 14**
- Guzik quotes two scholars on why killing the heir seemed worth it. Jeremias (cited by Pate) thinks the tenants may have assumed the owner had died. Morris says land could be presumed owned after three years' use. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Guzik also says the parable shows Jesus knew He was the Son and would soon be killed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks some Sanhedrin members knew exactly who Jesus claimed to be and sinned against their own consciences. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm

**v. 15**
- Utley: Jesus was killed outside Jerusalem's walls. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- Wuest (quoted by Precept Austin) says "threw him out" pictures Israel's leaders excommunicating Jesus. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary

**v. 16**
- **"May such a thing never happen!"** Ellicott says the Greek doesn't mention God. It is like a "negative Amen" ("so be it not"), and Paul uses it often. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Guzik: the hearers thought, "This could never be us." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- Matthew Henry calls their cry a "cold *God forbid*" that does nothing to prevent the judgment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**v. 17**
- **"Looked directly at them."** Ellicott says the verb means a fixed gaze. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Guzik says Psalm 118 describes the Messiah coming to Jerusalem. He explains "cornerstone" as the key stone that carries the building's weight. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary says the tenants have now become "builders," and the murdered son has become the rejected stone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott notes that this verse is missing from many good manuscripts of Matthew but appears in all manuscripts of Luke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- The commentators read the two halves of the verse in different ways:
  - **Guzik:** whoever comes to Jesus is broken of pride; whoever refuses is crushed in judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
  - **Matthew Henry:** "broken" means careless unbelievers; "crushed" means those who hate and persecute Him, whose judgment is heavier. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm
  - **Pulpit Commentary:** the stone laid in the earth pictures Christ's humiliation; the stone falling pictures Him crushing all opposition in His glory. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm

**vv. 16–18: where the sources differ on Israel**
- **Matthew Henry:** the Jewish nation provoked God to take away from them all their church privileges. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm
- **Gill:** God would "unchurch" them and raise up a church among the Gentiles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-9.htm
- **Precept Austin** looks ahead to a future earthly reign, when the Messiah will be the Head of the Millennial empire, the Headstone of the Corner. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-20-commentary
- **Utley** says it's hard to tell whether God was rejecting Israel's illegitimate high priests, its legalism, or the unbelief of the whole nation. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20

**v. 19**
- The Pulpit Commentary says the crowds, swelled by Passover pilgrims, treated Jesus as a hero. The council felt its power slipping away. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Gill applies the verse: enemies of Christ's people often portray them as a danger to the government. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-19.htm

**v. 20**
- **"Spies."** Ellicott says the word is found only in Luke and means people lying in ambush. He says Luke is the clearest about the aim: material for a charge before Pilate. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Sanhedrin decided to use the hated Roman authorities. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/20-20.htm
- Matthew Henry says persecuting religious leaders have often used rulers to do their dirty work. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**v. 21**
- Guzik calls this "obvious and clumsy" flattery. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Homiletics speaks of The worthlessness of heartless praise. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-20.html
- Ellicott notes that the same phrase ("accept the person") appears in Galatians 2:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm

**v. 22**
- **The trap.** Guzik: saying "yes" would look like denying God's rule over Israel; saying "no" would make Jesus Rome's enemy. Zealots refused to pay; most Jews paid reluctantly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary says this was a head tax of one denarius per person. Matthew and Mark show the Herodians teaming up with the Pharisees. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm

**v. 23**
- **"Duplicity."** Ellicott says this Greek word appears only here in the Gospels; Paul uses it four times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/luke/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jesus knew their hearts even though they spoke fairly. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**v. 24**
- **The coin.** Utley says it bore Tiberius's image, called him son of the divine Augustus, and called him "Highest Priest" on the back, which claimed divinity for Caesar. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-20
- Guzik (quoting Pate) says a coin's image worked like a property seal. Using Caesar's coins meant accepting his civil authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-20/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the questioners may have had to borrow the coin from money-changers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/20.htm
- Matthew Henry: once they used Caesar's money in trade, they had already accepted his rule. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_020.cfm

**vv. 22–24: where traditions differ on church and state**
These sources mostly comment on the answer in v. 25, but they read the coin question through it:
- **Lutheran:** an LCMS Bible study uses "render to Caesar" to teach the two kingdoms. It says there are two kingdoms but only one King, and it treats confusing the two as a failure to distinguish Law and Gospel. https://witness.lcms.org/2012/two-kinds-of-authority-a-bible-study-4-2012/
- **Reformed:** R. C. Sproul preached on Luke 20:19–26. One of his headings is "Even Unjust Taxes Must Be Paid," and he points to early Christians who died rather than worship Caesar. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/render-unto-caesar
- **Guzik:** obey the government in civil matters, but obey God first when the state claims what belongs to Him. https://enduringword.com/blog-archive/qa-transcripts/what-did-jesus-mean-by-give-to-caesar-what-is-caesars-live-qa-for-may-15-2025/
- **Godet** (cited in the Pulpit Commentary): Israel would regain its freedom by faithfulness to God, not by revolt. https://biblehub.com/luke/20-25.htm
